summary: Year 6 learners derive and apply area formulae for parallelograms (A = base × perpendicular height) and triangles (A = ½ × base × perpendicular height) through dissection rather than being told the rules. A parallelogram is cut and rearranged into an equal-area rectangle; two congruent triangles are joined into a parallelogram so a triangle is seen to be exactly half (justifying the ÷2). The load-bearing ideas are: the height must be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the chosen base (not a slant side), any side can be the base with its own matching perpendicular height, and the halving step follows from the dissection rather than being an arbitrary rule. Decoy slant lengths teach that a 'given' number is not always a 'needed' number.
misconceptions: Uses the slant side instead of the perpendicular height, partly from believing every number given must be used.
Forgets to halve for a triangle (computes base × height and stops).
Thinks the base must be the horizontal or bottom side, so cannot identify base and height in rotated or obtuse triangles.

activities.title: Dissection workbench: rearrange to reveal the formulae
steps: Take a parallelogram whose perpendicular height from a top corner lands on the base. Cut along that height to remove a right-angled triangle, then slide it to the other end so it forms a rectangle of the SAME area. Confirm that base × perpendicular height is the area, because the rectangle's length and width are the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height.
Take a triangle, duplicate and rotate the copy, and fit the two copies together into a parallelogram; observe that the single triangle is exactly HALF, so its area is base × perpendicular height ÷ 2.
Place or drag the height line so it meets the base at 90°, marking the right angle; check a line that is NOT perpendicular and explain why it is not the height.
Rotate the shape so the base is no longer horizontal, then identify which side is now the base and where its perpendicular height falls.
Work with a diagram that includes a decoy slant length (e.g. base 7, perpendicular height 6, slant 8) and deliberately ignore the slant when computing the area.
activities.insight: The area formulae are consequences of rearranging shapes: a parallelogram is a rectangle in disguise, and a triangle is half a parallelogram, which is where the ÷2 comes from. The height is always perpendicular to whichever side is chosen as the base, and not every given number is needed.

activities.title: Paper-and-scissors dissection (hands-on alternative)
steps: Cut out a paper parallelogram, draw its perpendicular height, snip along it to remove a right-angled triangle and slide it across to physically make a rectangle; measure the rectangle's length and width and compare them with the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height.
Cut two identical paper triangles and fit them together to make a parallelogram or rectangle; state in words why one triangle is half.
Physically turn a triangle so a different side is the base, then draw the perpendicular height from the opposite vertex to that base and mark the right angle.
activities.insight: Physically cutting and rearranging makes the equal-area and 'half of a parallelogram' relationships concrete, and turning the paper shape shows the base does not have to be horizontal.

activities.title: 'Who is right?' and calculation practice with decoy lengths
steps: Compute the area of a triangle given a base, a marked perpendicular height and a decoy slant length, choosing the correct length and halving (e.g. base 7, perpendicular height 6, slant 8 → 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm²).
Compute the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm, halving the product: 12 × 7 ÷ 2 = 42 cm².
Decide in a 'who is right?' task which of two learners picked the correct length for the height, and justify the choice using the right-angle mark.

Complete a worked step that forces the ÷2 explicitly, and separately compute a parallelogram area without halving (e.g. base 8, perpendicular height 5 → 40 cm²) to show that ÷2 is NOT applied to parallelograms.
activities.insight: Fluency in selecting the perpendicular height, ignoring unnecessary numbers, and applying the ÷2 only to triangles, while being able to justify each choice.

activities.title: Diagnostic: two shapes with decoy slants
steps: Given a triangle labelled base 7 cm, perpendicular height 6 cm (right angle marked to the base) and slant side 8 cm, find its area.
Given a parallelogram with base 8 cm, perpendicular height 5 cm and a longer slant side shown, find its area.
Explain aloud which lengths were used and why: why the triangle is halved and the parallelogram is not, and why the 8 cm slant was ignored.
activities.insight: Demonstrates relational understanding: selecting the perpendicular height, ignoring the decoy, halving only the triangle, and justifying the ½ via two-triangles-make-a-parallelogram.

checkQuestion: Hand the child a triangle labelled base 7 cm, perpendicular height 6 cm (right angle marked to the base) and a slant side 8 cm, plus a parallelogram with base 8 cm, perpendicular height 5 cm and a longer slant side shown. Say: 'Find the area of each.' Then WATCH which lengths they choose, whether they use the perpendicular height rather than the 8 cm slant, whether they halve for the triangle, and whether they can say why.
checkAnswer: Triangle area = 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm² (uses the perpendicular height, ignores the 8 cm slant, halves); parallelogram area = 8 × 5 = 40 cm² (base × perpendicular height, not the slant).
